name: Dr Macaura's blood circulator

image.caption: Dr Macaura's Blood Circulator. Wellcome L0010304

lead: Dr Macaura's blood circulator was a hand-cranked mechanical vibrator made between 1890 and 1910 in Leeds, England. It was advertised as stimulating blood circulation, and cranking the handle produced about 2,000 vibrations per minute applied to the body.
It appears in beauty and health history as a forerunner of vibration and circulation-boosting devices. It is preserved in the Science Museum Group collection.

paras: The user cranked a handle so the rubber-headed attachments vibrated against the body.
No safety record is documented. Its advertised cures were broad and the inventor himself conceded it did not help cancer, tuberculosis or baldness.

lead: Dr Macaura's blood circulator was a hand-cranked mechanical massager made between 1890 and 1910 in Leeds by the British Appliances Manufacturing Company; it is held by the Science Museum Group [1]. Cranking the handle produced two thousand vibrations per minute, and the device was applied to the body [1].

It was advertised as a blood circulator for conditions including pain, deafness, anaemia, heart disease and cramp; the inventor, Gerald (or Gerard) Joseph Macaura, said it could not help cancer, tuberculosis or baldness and advised good diet, deep breathing and avoiding alcohol [1]. Thousands were made [1].
infobox: Steel, nickel, vulcanite, lignum vitae, rubber

paras: The Science Museum object is made of steel, nickel plating, vulcanite, lignum vitae wood and rubber heads and came with a cardboard box [1]. It belongs to the therapeutics collection from Sir Henry Wellcome's museum [1]. A second catalogued version with attachments lists Footman and Company as maker and a chiropody category [2].
